The Aardvark Migration Study

Over the past decade the Serengeti Wildlife Journal has tracked more than four hundred nocturnal aardvarks across the miombo woodland corridor, and the results overturn a long-held assumption. Far from being strictly solitary and sedentary, tagged individuals routinely travelled between eleven and nineteen kilometres in a single night in pursuit of shifting termite colonies. This roaming behaviour intensified sharply in the weeks following the first rains, when subterranean insect activity peaks.

The tracking programme relied on lightweight satellite collars that transmitted a fix every ninety minutes. Analysts cross-referenced the movement data against soil-moisture readings and found a striking correlation: aardvarks abandoned a burrow within seventy-two hours of the surrounding soil drying below a critical threshold. In effect, the animals are chasing the water table, not merely foraging at random.

Perhaps the most surprising finding concerns social tolerance. On at least thirty documented occasions, two unrelated adults shared the same burrow network for several consecutive days without conflict — a degree of cohabitation never previously recorded for the species. The authors argue that these findings should reshape how protected corridors are drawn, because a reserve sized for a sedentary animal will fail an animal that ranges this widely.
